questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Nudges, and whether they're used for good
How to stop buying things online
Why governments ban advertising
How to win a Nobel Prize in economics like Richard Thaler
questions.why: They ask whether the idea behind nudging – to influence behaviour for good – is still true today.

questions.q: How might a supermarket nudge people to eat better?
options: By making chocolate bars much more expensive than fruit
By placing healthy snacks where they're easy to reach
By sending shoppers text messages
By refusing to sell sweets
questions.why: Neil describes healthy snacks near the checkout and chocolate hidden on the top shelf.

questions.q: What concern does Beth raise about nudging?
options: It doesn't work on most people
It is far too expensive for most governments to use
It is only used by doctors
It is often used to make money for big companies
questions.why: She says nudging is often used less to benefit society and more to make money for big business.

options: With an advertising campaign by Ogilvy in London
With a social media company's experiment
With a 2008 book by economist Richard Thaler
With a government law in 2011
questions.why: Neil says nudging started in 2008 with a book by Professor Richard Thaler.

questions.q: What example does Rory Sutherland give?
options: Painting pictures on shop windows
Making the profitable button green and the other one grey
Sending people text reminders about their doctor's appointments
Saying there is “only one left”
questions.why: He describes making the profitable option green and attractive and the other grey and manky.

questions.q: Why does Rory Sutherland give this example?
options: To show a nudge that isn't always good for the customer
To show how nudges can help people save money on shopping
To explain why green is a popular colour
To prove that nudges never work online
questions.why: He calls it a nudge “not necessarily used in the best interests of the consumer”.

questions.q: What is Professor Neil Levy's main criticism of nudging?
options: It is far too slow to change how people actually behave
It only benefits governments
It decides for us when we want to make our own choices
It is based on bad science
questions.why: He says it's paternalistic: nudges might be in our interests, but we want to make our own decisions.

questions.q: What does Neil the presenter conclude about nudging?
options: It should be banned
It is always good for society
It is mostly harmless fun that nobody really notices
Whether it's good or bad depends on how it's used
questions.why: He says nudging itself is neither good nor bad, it just depends how you use it.
